posts.content:
Introducing Supabase Pipelines.

Your app runs on Postgres. Your analytics usually run somewhere else, like a data warehouse, and getting your data there reliably has meant building and maintaining your own pipeline.

Supabase Pipelines does that for you. You pick a destination in the dashboard, and we run and monitor a managed pipeline that replicates your Postgres data there in near real time. It's built on Postgres logical replication and powered by Supabase ETL.

It runs an initial sync of your tables, then replicates every insert, update, delete, and truncate, and keeps your destination schema in sync as your Postgres schema changes.

Read more: https://lnkd.in/dXD_PAKV

posts.content:
I never thought I'd ship a production app. I'm a product manager, not an engineer. This week I did, and I'm insanely proud of it.

dokita is an app that helps Swiss daycares document each child's development. The whole team at the Spielhuus Schnäggli daycare (Kita) in St. Gallen now documents over 50 children with it every day, and they report up to 80% less documentation time.

The idea found me during my son's settling-in weeks at exactly this Kita. I was there often and got a rare look at daily life in a daycare and at everything the educators take on. Much of the documentation was done by hand, often in the evening once the children had gone home. So I built a first prototype, tested it with the team and kept improving it with their feedback.

Stefan, who leads the Kita, puts it like this: "It has become easier to stay on top of certain topics, and the documentation itself encourages us to keep reflecting on our pedagogical work." (translated from German)

I know what the engineers among you are thinking. Yet another vibe-coded AI app. So here is what's under the hood: a git repo with a proper branching strategy, a staging environment with a local test database, automated linting and end-to-end tests, code review by three different coding agents, and over 150 merged PRs (still counting). And because children's data is about the most sensitive data there is, the app complies with Swiss data protection, confirmed by an external security review.

I don't have a computer science background. I was always drawn to tech but never confident enough to study it or teach it to myself. AI turned out to be the missing piece. I started in Lovable and moved to Claude Code (Anthropic), Supabase and Vercel for the app. With Claude Design I built the brand, from the logo to the website, and that part was a delight. Add many years of product sense, and one person can take an idea from first sketch to production, brand and website included.

I lived through, on my own product, how the product manager job is changing: from writing specs and handing off to building end to end. I learned a ton and enjoyed every bit of it.

dokita.ch is live, and the demo works without an account.

I'm considering coaching a handful of PMs through exactly this, from prototype to a real product. If that's you, send me a message.

#ProductManagement #BuildInPublic #AIProductBuilding #SwissTech

posts.content:
For a long time, debugging across the boundary between your app and Supabase meant treating them as two separate systems. A slow request in your frontend trace and the matching log in Supabase had nothing connecting them, so you lined them up by hand, guessing at timestamps.

That gap is closed. supabase-js, Swift, Flutter, and Python now propagate W3C Trace Context to Supabase. Turn it on and the SDK attaches standard trace headers to every Supabase-bound request, Supabase stamps that same 𝚝𝚛𝚊𝚌𝚎_𝚒𝚍 onto the API Gateway and Edge Function logs it generates. Any W3C-compliant tracer, OpenTelemetry, Sentry, Datadog, Honeycomb, Grafana, picks the trace back up on the server side, no new tooling required.

If you already run Log Drains, this is where it pays off: every drained log now carries the same 𝚝𝚛𝚊𝚌𝚎_𝚒𝚍, so it joins the rest of your trace in whatever tool you already use, at no extra cost.

Available now.

Read more: https://lnkd.in/gqMWNRyy

article.title: The Drew Crew | Supabase Customer Stories
article.subtitle: supabase.com
article.linkLabel: Open article: The Drew Crew | Supabase Customer Stories by supabase.com

posts.content:
Today we're open-sourcing Supabase Evals, our benchmark for how well AI coding agents build with Supabase.

Agents are now a primary way people build with Supabase, through our MCP server, CLI, agent skills, and docs. Until now we measured how well that worked with manual testing and intuition. Supabase Evals measures that experience instead of guessing.

It runs coding agents like Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode against real Supabase tasks, such as building a schema, debugging a failed Edge Function, or fixing a broken RLS policy, then scores what they actually did. Every scenario runs against a real Supabase environment, so agents call our actual MCP server and CLI.

A few things worth knowing:
- Scenarios come from real pain points: support tickets, bug reports, and GitHub issues
- Scoring mixes deterministic checks with LLM-as-judge
- Browse and filter results by model, product, stage, or eval
- Open source, so the scenarios and scoring criteria are there to inspect

Available now.

posts.content:
Postgres Changes now supports AND filters, more filter operators, and column selection.

Postgres Changes lets you listen to row-level inserts, updates, and deletes over a WebSocket. Filters now compose with AND on a single subscription, and the operator set is closer to the filter syntax you already use elsewhere in Supabase.

You can also choose which columns land in the payload. Column filters can't be evaluated on deletes, since a DELETE event only carries the row's primary key.

A few things worth knowing:
- Combine filters with a comma: filter: '𝚜𝚝𝚊𝚝𝚞𝚜=𝚎𝚚.𝚍𝚘𝚗𝚎,𝚙𝚛𝚒𝚘𝚛𝚒𝚝𝚢=𝚎𝚚.𝚑𝚒𝚐𝚑'
- New operators: 𝚕𝚒𝚔𝚎, 𝚒𝚕𝚒𝚔𝚎, 𝚒𝚜, 𝚖𝚊𝚝𝚌𝚑, 𝚒𝚖𝚊𝚝𝚌𝚑, 𝚒𝚜𝚍𝚒𝚜𝚝𝚒𝚗𝚌𝚝, and a 𝚗𝚘𝚝. prefix to negate any of them
- Column selection is opt in. It needs @supabase/supabase-js 2.109.0 or newer; the filter changes work with what you already have

Available now.
